newsitem.title: YEMEN: South Yemenis give former president warm welcome.
newsitem.headline: South Yemenis give former president warm welcome.

text.p: Former South Yemen president Ali Nasser Mohammed returned to Aden on Thursday for first time since he was ousted in a bloody 1986 coup.

Thousands of people, many waiving pictures of Mohammed who still wields political influence in south Yemen, watched as the plane sent by Yemeni President Ali Abdullah Saleh to carry him from Damascus landed in Aden.

Yemen's central security force chief Mohammad Abdullah Saleh, a brother of the Yemeni president, and local government officials welcomed the 57-year-old Mohammed and his eldest son Jamal as they stepped out of the presidential aircraft.
But hundreds of men who got into the airport past heavy security had no time to shake hands with Mohammed before he was whisked away to a guest palace. Journalists were prevented from talking to him.

"Welcome home Ali Nasser," chanted some in the crowd as his heavily-guarded motorcade drove past. Many had waited hours in the main street to the airport to catch a glimpse of the man who once ruled this southern port city.
Mohammed, in an interview with Reuters on Wednesday at his residence in the Syrian capital Damascus, said he was not thinking now of any government post or of staying in Yemen permanently.

"I experienced authority and was burned by its fire...in the past I took the jobs of a governor, a minister, a prime minister, a vice-president and a president," he said. "But now my concern is to develop the Arab Centre for Strategic Studies which I chair."

Mohammed was ousted from power in South Yemen in January 1986 after bloody fighting with forces of Ali Salem al-Baidh, who signed a unity treaty with North Yemen in 1989. Baidh was defeated in a 1994 civil war by Saleh and forced to flee the country.
Yemeni sources say Mohammed, whose supporters hold senior posts in Saleh's government, could help ease tension between political parties in north and south Yemen caused by the 1994 civil war.
Mohammed, who last year established the centre for Arab strategic studies with Damascus as its headquarters, said he would open a branch in the Yemeni capital Sanaa during his visit.
He said there were no plans for a branch in Aden although this might be done when financial resources were available.
The former president said he would meet Saleh and take part in celebrations of the 29th anniversary of independence and the seventh anniversary of the unity treaty.
Mohammed began his career as governor of the Yemen Islands immediately after independence from Britain in 1967. In 1969 he was named minister of local adminstration.
In 1970 he became defence minister and in 1971 prime minister. He was vice-president between 1971 and 1978. He was president from 1980 until ousted in 1986.
